{{Short description|none}}
This is a glossary of concepts and results in [[number theory]], a field of [[mathematics]]. Concepts and results in [[arithmetic geometry]] and [[diophantine geometry]] can be found in [[Glossary of arithmetic and diophantine geometry]].

See also [[List of number theory topics]].

{{compact ToC|side=yes|top=yes|num=yes}}

== A ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|abc conjecture}}
{{defn|1=The [[abc conjecture]] says that for all {{math|''ε'' > 0}}, there are only finitely many coprime positive integers {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}}, and {{math|''c''}} satisfying {{math|1=''a''+''b''=''c''}} such that the product of the distinct prime factors of {{math|''abc''}} raised to the power of {{math|1+''ε''}} is less than {{math|''c''}}.}}

{{term|adele}}
{{defn|[[Adele ring]]}}

{{term|algebraic number}}
{{defn|An [[algebraic number]] is a number that is the root of some non-zero polynomial in one variable with integer (or, equivalently, rational) coefficients.}}

{{term|algebraic number field}}
{{defn|See number field.}}

{{term|algebraic number theory}}
{{defn|[[Algebraic number theory]]}}

{{term|analytic number theory}}
{{defn|[[Analytic number theory]]}}

{{term|Artin}}
{{defn|1=The [[Artin conjecture (L-functions)|Artin conjecture]] says [[Artin's L function]] is entire (holomorphic on the entire complex plane).}}

{{term|automorphic form}}
{{defn|An [[automorphic form]] is a certain holomorphic function.}}

{{glossary end}}

== B ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Bézout's identity}}
{{defn|[[Bézout's identity]], also called Bézout's lemma, states that if {{math|''d''}} is the greatest common divisor of two integers {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''b''}}, then there exists integers {{math|''x''}} and {{math|''y''}} such that {{math|1=''ax'' + ''by'' = ''d''}}, and in fact the integers of the form {{math|''as'' + ''bt''}} are exactly the multiples of {{math|''d''}}.}}

{{term|Brocard}}
{{defn|1=[[Brocard's problem]]}}
{{glossary end}}

== C ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Chinese remainder theorem}}
{{defn|[[Chinese remainder theorem]]}}

{{term|class field}}
{{defn|The [[class field theory]] concerns abelian extensions of number fields.}}

{{term|class number}}
{{defn|no=1|1=The [[class number (number theory)|class number]] of a number field is the cardinality of the ideal class group of the field.}}
{{defn|no=2|1=In group theory, the [[class number (group theory)|class number]] is the number of conjugacy classes of a group.}}
{{defn|no=3|1=[[Class number (binary quadratic forms)|Class number]] is the number of equivalence classes of binary quadratic forms of a given discriminant.}}
{{defn|no=4|1=The [[class number problem]].}}

{{term|conductor}}
{{defn|[[Conductor (class field theory)]]}}

{{term|coprime}}
{{defn|Two integers are [[coprime]] (also called relatively prime) if the only positive integer that divides them both is 1.}}

{{glossary end}}

== D ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Dedekind}}
{{defn|[[Dedekind zeta function]].}}

{{term|Diophantine equation}}
{{defn|[[Diophantine equation]]}}

{{term|Dirichlet}}
{{defn|no=1|[[Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions]]}}
{{defn|no=2|1=[[Dirichlet character]]}}
{{defn|no=3|1=[[Dirichlet's unit theorem]].}}

{{term|distribution}}
{{defn|1=A [[distribution (number theory)|distribution in number theory]] is a generalization/variant of a distribution in analysis.}}

{{term|divisor}}
{{defn|A [[divisor]] or factor of an integer {{math|''n''}} is an integer {{math|''m''}} such that there exists an integer {{math|''k''}} satisfying {{math|1=''n'' = ''mk''}}. Divisors can be defined in exactly the same way for polynomials or for elements of a commutative ring.}}

{{glossary end}}

== E ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Eisenstein}}
{{defn|[[Eisenstein series]]}}

{{term|elliptic curve}}
{{defn|[[Elliptic curve]]}}

{{term|Erdős}}
{{defn|1=[[Erdős–Kac theorem]]}}

{{term|Euclid's lemma}}
{{defn|[[Euclid's lemma]] states that if a prime {{math|''p''}} divides the product of two integers {{math|''ab''}}, then {{math|''p''}} must divide at least one of {{math|''a''}} or {{math|''b''}}.}}

{{term|Euler's criterion}}
{{defn|Let {{math|''p''}} is an odd prime and {{math|''a''}} is an integer not divisible by {{math|''p''}}. [[Euler's criterion]] provides a slick way to determine whether {{math|''a''}} is a quadratic residue mod {{math|''p''}}. It says that <math>a^{\tfrac{p-1}{2}}</math> is congruent to 1 mod {{math|''p''}} if {{math|''a''}} is a quadratic residue mod {{math|''p''}} and is congruent to -1 mod {{math|''p''}} if not. This can be written using Legendre symbols as
:<math>\left(\frac{a}{p}\right) \equiv a^{\tfrac{p-1}{2}} \pmod p.</math>}}

{{term|Euler's theorem}}
{{defn|[[Euler's theorem]] states that if {{math|''n''}} and {{math|''a''}} are coprime positive integers, then {{math|''a''<sup>''φ''(''n'')</sup>}} is congruent to {{math|1}} mod {{math|''n''}}. Euler's theorem generalizes Fermat's little theorem.}}

{{term|Euler's totient function}}
{{defn|For a positive integer {{math|''n''}}, [[Euler's totient function]] of {{math|''n''}}, denoted {{math|''φ''(''n'')}}, is the number of integers coprime to {{math|''n''}} between {{math|1}} and {{math|''n''}} inclusive. For example, {{math|1=''φ''(4) = 2}} and {{math|1=''φ''(''p'') = ''p'' - 1}} for any prime {{math|''p''}}.}}

{{glossary end}}

== F ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|factor}}
{{defn|See the entry for divisor.}}

{{term|factorization}}
{{defn|[[Factorization]] is the process of splitting a mathematical object, often integers or polynomials, into a product of factors.}}

{{term|Fermat's Last Theorem}}
{{defn|[[Fermat's Last Theorem]], one of the most famous and difficult to prove theorems in number theory, states that for any integer {{math|''n'' > 2}}, the equation {{math|1=''a''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''b''<sup>''n''</sup> = ''c''<sup>''n''</sup>}} has no positive integer solutions.}}

{{term|Fermat's little theorem}}
{{defn|[[Fermat's little theorem]]}}

{{term|field extension}}
{{defn|A [[field extension]] {{math|''L''/''K''}} is a pair of fields {{math|''K''}} and {{math|''L''}} such that {{math|''K''}} is a subfield of {{math|''L''}}. Given a field extension {{math|''L''/''K''}}, the field {{math|''L''}} is a {{math|''K''}}-vector space.}}

{{term|fundamental theorem of arithmetic}}
{{defn|The [[fundamental theorem of arithmetic]] states that every integer greater than 1 can be written uniquely (up to reordering) as a product of primes.}}

{{glossary end}}

== G ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Galois}}
{{defn|A [[Galois extension]] is a finite field extension {{math|''L''/''K''}} such that one of the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:
*{{math|''L''/''K''}} is a [[normal extension]] and a [[separable extension]],
*{{math|''L''}} is a [[splitting field]] of a [[separable polynomial]] with coefficients in {{math|''K''}},
*{{math|1={{!}}Aut(''L''/''K''){{!}} = [''L'':''K'']}}, that is, the number of automorphisms of the extension equals its [[degree (field theory)|degree]].
The automorphism group {{math|1=Aut(''L''/''K'')}} of a Galois extension is called its [[Galois group]] and it is denoted {{math|1=Gal(''L''/''K'').}}}}

{{term|global field}}
{{defn|[[Global field]]}}

{{term|Goldbach's conjecture}}
{{defn|[[Goldbach's conjecture]] is a conjecture that states that every even natural number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes.}}

{{term|greatest common divisor}}
{{defn|The [[greatest common divisor]] of a finite list of integers is the largest positive number that is a divisor of every integer in the list.}}

{{glossary end}}

== H ==
{{glossary}}

{{term|Hasse}}
{{defn|[[Hasse's theorem on elliptic curves]].}}

{{term|Hecke}}
{{defn|[[Hecke algebra|Hecke ring]]}}

{{glossary end}}

== I ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|ideal}}
{{defn|The [[ideal class group]] of a number field is the group of fractional ideals in the ring of integers in the field modulo principal ideals. The cardinality of the group is called the class number of the number field. It measures the extent of the failure of unique factorization.}}

{{term|integer}}
{{defn|no=1|The [[integer]]s are the numbers {{math|…, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …}}.}}
{{defn|no=2|In algebraic number theory, an integer sometimes means an element of a ring of integers; e.g., a [[Gaussian integer]]. To avoid ambiguity, an integer contained in <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> is sometimes called a rational integer.}}

{{term|Iwasawa}}
{{defn|[[Iwasawa theory]]}}

{{glossary end}}

== L ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Langlands}}
{{defn|1=[[Langlands program]]}}

{{term|least common multiple}}
{{defn|The [[least common multiple]] of a finite list of integers is the smallest positive number that is a multiple of every integer in the list.}}

{{term|Legendre symbol}}
{{defn|1=Let {{math|''p''}} be an odd prime and let {{math|''a''}} be an integer. The [[Legendre symbol]] of {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''p''}} is
:<math>\left(\frac{a}{p}\right) = 
\begin{cases}
 1 & \text{if } a \text{ is a quadratic residue mod } p \text{ and } a \not\equiv 0\pmod p, \\
-1 & \text{if } a \text{ is not a quadratic residue mod } p \text{ and } a \not\equiv 0\pmod p, \\
 0 & \text{if } a \equiv 0 \pmod p.
\end{cases}</math>
The Legendre symbol provides a convenient notational package for several results, including the law of quadratic reciprocity and Euler's criterion.
}}

{{term|local}}
{{defn|no=1|A [[local field]] in number theory is the completion of a number field at a finite place.}}
{{defn|no=2|The [[local–global principle]].}}

{{glossary end}}

== M ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Mersenne prime}}
{{defn|A [[Mersenne prime]] is a prime number one less than a power of 2.}}

{{term|modular form}}
{{defn|[[Modular form]]}}

{{term|modularity theorem}}
{{defn|The [[modularity theorem]] (which used to be called the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture)}}

{{glossary end}}

== N ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|number field}}
{{defn|A [[Algebraic number field|number field]], also called an algebraic number field, is a finite-degree field extension of the field of rational numbers.}}

{{term|non-abelian}}
{{defn|The [[non-abelian class field theory]] is an extension of the class field theory (which is about abelian extensions of number fields) to non-abelian extensions; or at least the idea of such a theory. The non-abelian theory does not exist in a definitive form today.}}

{{glossary end}}

== P ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Pell's equation}}
{{defn|[[Pell's equation]]}}

{{term|period}}
{{defn|1=[[period conjecture]]}}

{{term|place}}
{{defn|A [[place (number theory)|place]] is an equivalence class of non-Archimedean valuations (finite place) or absolute values (infinite place).}}

{{term|prime number}}
{{defn|no=1|A [[prime number]] is a positive integer with no divisors other than itself and 1.}}
{{defn|no=2|The [[prime number theorem]] describes the asymptotic distribution of prime numbers.}}

{{term|profinite}}
{{defn|1=A [[profinite integer]] is an element in the profinite completion <math>\widehat{\mathbb Z}</math> of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> along all integers.}}

{{term|Pythagorean triple}}
{{defn|A [[Pythagorean triple]] is three positive integers {{math|''a'', ''b'', ''c''}} such that {{math|1=''a''{{sup|2}} + ''b''{{sup|2}} = ''c''{{sup|2}}}}.}}

{{glossary end}}

== R ==
{{glossary}}

{{term|ramification}}
{{defn|The [[ramification theory]].}}

{{term|relatively prime}}
{{defn|See coprime.}}

{{term|ring of integers}}
{{defn|1=The [[ring of integers]] in a number field is the ring consisting of all [[algebraic number]]s contained in the field.}}

{{glossary end}}

== Q ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|quadratic reciprocity}}
{{defn|Let ''p'' and ''q'' be distinct odd prime numbers, and define the [[Legendre symbol]] as
:<math>\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)
=\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } n^2 \equiv q \bmod p \text{ for some integer } n\\
-1 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}</math>
The law of [[quadratic reciprocity]] states that
:<math> \left(\frac{p}{q}\right) \left(\frac{q}{p}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}\frac{q-1}{2}}.</math>
This result aids in the computation of Legendre symbols and thus helps determine whether an integer is a quadratic residue.
}}

{{term|quadratic residue}}
{{defn|An integer {{math|''q''}} is called a [[quadratic residue]] mod {{math|''n''}} if it is congruent to a perfect square mod {{math|''n''}}, i.e., if there exists an integer {{math|''x''}} such that <math>x^2\equiv q \pmod{n}.</math>}}

{{glossary end}}

== S ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|sieve of Eratosthenes}}
{{defn|[[Sieve of Eratosthenes]]}}

{{term|square-free integer}}
{{defn|A [[square-free integer]] is an integer that is not divisible by any square other than 1.}}

{{term|square number}}
{{defn|A [[square number]] is an integer that is the square of an integer. For example, 4 and 9 are squares, but 10 is not a square.}}

{{term|Szpiro}}
{{defn|1=[[Szpiro's conjecture]] is, in a modified form, equivalent to the abc conjecture.}}

{{glossary end}}

== T ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Takagi}}
{{defn|[[Takagi existence theorem]] is a theorem in class field theory.}}

{{term|totient function}}
{{defn|See Euler's totient function.}}

{{term|twin prime}}
{{defn|A [[twin prime]] is a prime number that is 2 less or 2 more than another prime number. For example, 7 is a twin prime, since it is prime and 5 is also prime.}}

{{glossary end}}

== V ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|valuation}}
{{defn|[[valuation (algebra)]]}}

{{term|valued field}}
{{defn|A [[valued field]] is a field with a valuation on it.}}

{{term|1=Vojta}}
{{defn|1=[[Vojta's conjecture]]}}

{{glossary end}}

== W ==

{{glossary}}

{{term|Wilson's theorem}}
{{defn|[[Wilson's theorem]] states that {{math|1=''n'' > 1}} is prime if and only if {{math|(''n''-1)!}} is congruent to {{math|-1}} mod {{math|''n''}}.}}

{{glossary end}}
